extracted_by: hand, T-0313 — the Democrat read, April 1834
note: Vol. I No. 19, the last issue printed on the paper's Tuesday line — corpus.json records the publication day moving to Wednesday after 8 April, and the imprint at claim c005 is the Tuesday line's last printing. This is the month's best issue for STOREFRONTS: a bakery placed against Newberry & Dole's store, Peter Cohen's own advertisement, Montgomery's shop placed against Cohen's, and the Democrat's own building on the corner of South Water and Clark. Sixteen of this issue's thirty-two column strips carry an independent Vision reading and the rest are Tesseract fallbacks; every claim below says what it could not read.

claims.notes: A BAKERY OPENS ON SOUTH WATER STREET, PLACED AGAINST NEWBERRY & DOLE'S STORE. This is a documented storefront with a street AND an anchor AND a direction — 'a few doors north of' — which is as much as any advertisement in this month gives, and it is the class of evidence T-0263 needs. Newberry & Dole are already in the corpus as forwarding and commission merchants, so the bakery is placed against a building the reconstruction can independently locate. The same advertisement runs again on 1834-04-23 (p4 c2, claim c003 there), which is the window this business is documented across.

business.trade: dry goods, clothing, groceries and liquors

claims.notes: PETER COHEN'S STORE ON SOUTH WATER STREET, and the fullest printing of his advertisement this corpus has. Cohen is the worked fixture's own first business (T-0257, 1835-07-01) and this is him fifteen months earlier on the same street, selling winter clothing, groceries and liquors — so the storefront is documented across a window that reaches the scene date and needs no survival liberty. The street is stated and no anchor is; the placement is street_only rather than a relative one invented from the neighbouring Philo Carpenter advertisement, which the strip runs into but does not join. It is L. W. Montgomery's boot and shoe shop (claim c003) that places itself against Cohen, not the other way about.

claims.notes: MONTGOMERY'S SHOP IS STILL NEXT DOOR TO COHEN'S, AND THE INITIALS ARE NOW TWO. T-0310 read this same advertisement on 1834-01-28 and could only recover 'W. MONTGOMERY'; this printing carries 'L. W. MONTGOMERY', which is the same man with a fuller signature rather than a second one — same trade, same anchor, same copy, same 19 December 1833 dateline. The pair Cohen/Montgomery is the strongest documented adjacency on South Water Street in this range: one storefront placed against another, both running continuously from December 1833 through April 1834.

claims.notes: A MANUFACTORY, NOT A STORE — and the town has few. Daniel Elston & Co.'s soap and candle works is the kind of building a reconstruction cannot infer from a plat: it needs kettles, a yard and a smell, and it is announced here as newly commenced in April 1834. THE SAME FIRM IS PUTTING UP A SMOKE HOUSE IN THE SAME MONTH — 'D. Elston & Co, who acquaint [the public] they have fitted up a Smoke [Hou]se, [for the smo]king of Hams, Bacon, &c.' (1834-04-30 p4 c2, claim c005 there) — so two separate works are being stood up under one name inside four weeks. No address is given in either, which is why both placements are `none` and not a guess; what is documented is that the works exist and when.

placement.anchor: the corner of South Water and Clark streets

claims.notes: THE NEWSPAPER'S OWN BUILDING, ON A NAMED CORNER. The imprint is the one advertisement in any issue whose subject is the press itself, and it places the office at the corner of South Water and Clark streets — a corner placement with both streets named, which is the strongest class this schema has. The reconstruction can therefore stand the Democrat's office on the ground rather than inferring it. The same imprint runs on 1834-04-30 (p4 c2 area) and on 1834-04-23 (p4 c8, 'corner of South, Water and Clarkst[reets]'), so the placement is corroborated three times inside the month. Note that the paper is still 'published every Tuesday' here while corpus.json records the printed publication day changing from Tuesday to Wednesday after 8 April — this issue IS 8 April, so the imprint is the last printing of the Tuesday line.

claims.notes: THE COURT WEEK IS WHEN THE COUNTY COMES TO TOWN. The Fountaindale Temperance Society, meeting in the country, appoints a committee to come to Chicago 'at the sitting of the Circuit Court' — because that is the week the rest of Cook County is already there. It is a small line and it says something the plat cannot: the town's population swelled on a court calendar, and the Circuit Court's sittings are the dates to hang that on. The society's own officers are named and are country residents, not townsmen, so they are recorded with that role rather than minted as Chicago people.
